stem: A 48-year-old man says his shoe size has gone up two sizes and his nose and hands have grown over 5 years, although his height has not changed. Serum IGF-1 is markedly elevated.
oneliner: 48M + shoe size up + nose and hands enlarging over 5 y + height unchanged + high IGF-1 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **growth excess before epiphyseal closure** gives tall stature; his height is unchanged
whyNot.B: **prolactin excess** gives hypogonadism and galactorrhea, not soft-tissue and bone overgrowth with high IGF-1
whyNot.D: can coarsen features, but **IGF-1 is not raised** and hands and shoes do not enlarge
whyNot.E: **focal** bone enlargement with high alkaline phosphatase; IGF-1 stays normal

why: **Acral growth in an adult with unchanged height** and **high IGF-1** = growth hormone excess after growth plates closed.

stem: A 52-year-old man notices that his face looks coarser and his nose has grown over several years. He has generalized muscle weakness and fatigue. He is not obese, has no skin striae and reports normal libido. Fasting glucose is 138 mg/dL and triglycerides are 290 mg/dL (normal <150). IGF-1 is markedly elevated.
oneliner: 52M + coarse face + enlarging nose + weakness + glucose 138 + TG 290 + high IGF-1 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: would give **central obesity and striae**; he has neither, and IGF-1 is not a cortisol marker
whyNot.C: gives coarse features but **low or normal IGF-1** and low metabolic rate, not hyperglycemia from GH
whyNot.D: requires **excess GH before growth plates close**; this is an adult
whyNot.E: **normal libido** and no galactorrhea described; prolactin excess does not raise IGF-1

why: **Coarse face and enlarging nose** with **high IGF-1**, hyperglycemia and hypertriglyceridemia = GH excess (insulin-antagonist effects).

stem: A 26-year-old woman has had headaches for 3 months and has had only three menstrual periods in the past year. She has milky discharge from both nipples. She has no weight gain or cold intolerance, and her pregnancy test is negative. Visual field testing shows loss of both temporal fields. An MRI of the brain is shown.
oneliner: 26F + headaches + galactorrhea + oligomenorrhea + bitemporal field loss + [MRI] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: usually a **calcified, cystic suprasellar mass**; mild prolactin rise from stalk effect rarely causes this much galactorrhea
whyNot.C: would show **coarse features and enlarging hands**, not galactorrhea and oligomenorrhea
whyNot.D: **dural-based** and not hormone-secreting; would not explain galactorrhea
whyNot.E: can raise prolactin, but she has **no weight gain or cold intolerance**, and it would not explain a sellar mass with chiasm compression

why: **Galactorrhea and oligomenorrhea** plus a **sellar mass compressing the chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia)** = prolactin-secreting macroadenoma.

image.prompt: Sagittal T1-weighted contrast MRI of the brain showing a rounded, solid, homogeneously enhancing 2-cm mass in the sella turcica that extends upward toward the optic chiasm, with no cysts or calcification. No labels or text.

stem: A 44-year-old man has had low libido and erectile dysfunction for a year, along with headaches and trouble seeing objects at the sides. Examination shows loss of both temporal visual fields, small soft testes and sparse body hair. Laboratory results: prolactin 1,850 ng/mL (normal <20), testosterone 90 ng/dL (normal 300-1,000), LH 1.1 mIU/mL, FSH 1.4 mIU/mL, IGF-1 normal. MRI shows a 3-cm pituitary mass.
oneliner: 44M + low libido + ED + headache + bitemporal field loss + testicular atrophy + prolactin 1,850 + low LH/FSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: stalk compression gives only a **mild prolactin rise (<100-150)**, not 1,850
whyNot.B: small testes but **LH and FSH are high**, and there is no pituitary mass
whyNot.C: **IGF-1 is normal** and there is no acral overgrowth
whyNot.E: produces only a **modest stalk-effect prolactin rise**, not a level near 2,000

why: **Prolactin 1,850 ng/mL** with a macroadenoma, low testosterone with low LH/FSH, and bitemporal field loss = prolactinoma.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has been unable to conceive for 2 years. Her periods were regular until 6 months ago, and she has had no menses since. She notices milky fluid from both nipples when she undresses. She takes no medications. Laboratory results: hCG negative, TSH 2.1 mU/L, FSH 4 mIU/mL, prolactin 120 ng/mL (normal <25).
oneliner: 31F + infertile + amenorrhea x6 mo + bilateral milky discharge + no drugs + hCG neg + TSH normal + prolactin 120 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: excluded by the **negative hCG**
whyNot.B: TSH is **normal at 2.1**
whyNot.C: gives hirsutism and anovulation but **not galactorrhea or prolactin of 120**
whyNot.D: FSH would be **high (>40)**; hers is low-normal

why: **Galactorrhea with amenorrhea** and **prolactin 120 ng/mL** without drugs, pregnancy or hypothyroidism = prolactinoma.

stem: A 33-year-old woman develops bilateral milky nipple discharge 3 weeks after starting metoclopramide for gastroparesis. She has no headaches or vision changes, her periods are regular, and her hCG and TSH are normal.
oneliner: 33F + bilateral milky discharge + metoclopramide x3 wk + no headache or vision change + hCG and TSH normal → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: a tumor would not be tied to the **start of the drug**; no headache or field defect
whyNot.B: **TSH is normal**
whyNot.D: **hCG is negative**
whyNot.E: does not cause galactorrhea, and her **cycles are regular**

why: **Galactorrhea beginning after metoclopramide** = loss of dopamine inhibition of prolactin release.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has been bumping into door frames on both sides for several weeks. She has had no periods for 4 months. She has no headache, and visual acuity is normal. Visual field testing shows loss of both temporal fields. Prolactin is 95 ng/mL, and MRI shows a homogeneously enhancing 1.5-cm mass in the sella with no calcification or cysts.
oneliner: 24F + amenorrhea x4 mo + gradual bitemporal field loss over weeks + prolactin 95 + 1.5-cm enhancing sellar mass → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: a **calcified, cystic** suprasellar mass; this lesion has no calcification or cysts
whyNot.C: arises from the **dura**, not within the sella
whyNot.D: gives **unilateral central** vision loss, not bitemporal
whyNot.E: presents with **sudden severe headache** and acute vision loss; hers is gradual and painless

why: **Bitemporal hemianopia** from chiasm compression plus a **sellar mass with raised prolactin** and amenorrhea = pituitary adenoma.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is seen 2 weeks after her first delivery, which was complicated by heavy bleeding and low blood pressure requiring transfusion. Her milk never came in. She feels tired and light-headed when she stands. She has no skin darkening, and her potassium is normal.
oneliner: 29F + 2 wk postpartum + hemorrhage with hypotension + no lactation + fatigue + orthostasis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: would cause **hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia**; she has neither
whyNot.C: would not explain **failure of lactation** or orthostasis
whyNot.D: does not cause **failure of milk production** or orthostatic symptoms
whyNot.E: autoimmune and **not triggered by hemorrhage**; usually presents with headache

why: **Postpartum hemorrhage** followed by **failure to lactate** and hypotensive symptoms = anterior pituitary infarction.

stem: A 38-year-old man has infertility and low libido 6 months after transsphenoidal removal of a nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma. He takes levothyroxine and hydrocortisone. He has a normal sense of smell. Semen analysis shows no sperm. Testosterone is 40 ng/dL (normal 300-1,000), with low LH and low FSH.
oneliner: 38M + infertile + low libido + after pituitary adenoma resection + azoospermia + low T + low LH/FSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: LH and FSH would be **high**, and onset is not after surgery
whyNot.B: gives **high LH and FSH**; his are low
whyNot.C: he had a **nonfunctioning** adenoma and no galactorrhea or tumor now; the problem is low gonadotropins from pituitary damage
whyNot.E: a congenital form with **anosmia**; his smell is normal and onset followed surgery

why: **Low testosterone with low LH and FSH** after pituitary surgery = secondary (pituitary) hypogonadism.

stem: A 35-year-old man is seen 3 weeks after a motor vehicle collision that caused a basilar skull fracture. He now drinks constantly and urinates large volumes, waking several times at night. Serum sodium is 146 mEq/L, glucose is normal, and urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg. After desmopressin, urine osmolality rises to 520 mOsm/kg.
oneliner: 35M + basilar skull fracture 3 wk ago + polyuria + polydipsia + Na 146 + urine osm 90 → rises to 520 with desmopressin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: sodium would be **low-normal**, not raised, and urine concentrates on water restriction
whyNot.B: gives **hyponatremia and concentrated urine**, the opposite of this picture
whyNot.C: urine **would not concentrate** after desmopressin
whyNot.D: osmotic diuresis needs **glycosuria**; his glucose is normal

why: **Skull-base trauma** with dilute urine that **concentrates after desmopressin** = ADH deficiency.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has a known suprasellar craniopharyngioma that is compressing the base of the brain. Over the past month she has been drinking 5 to 6 liters of water daily and passing large volumes of pale urine. Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L and glucose is normal. Urine osmolality rises after desmopressin.
oneliner: 26F + suprasellar craniopharyngioma + 5-6 L water/day + pale urine + Na 148 + urine concentrates with desmopressin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: sodium would be **low-normal** and urine would not need desmopressin to concentrate
whyNot.B: would give **low sodium and concentrated urine**
whyNot.C: kidneys **do respond** to desmopressin here
whyNot.E: her **glucose is normal**, so no osmotic diuresis

why: A **suprasellar tumor** damaging ADH release with **hypernatremia and desmopressin-responsive dilute urine** = central DI.

stem: A 12-year-old boy has new bed-wetting and now urinates 10 to 15 times a day, with a total output of 7.6 L daily. Urine osmolality is 230 mOsm/kg and urine specific gravity is low, while serum osmolality is 302 mOsm/kg. Urine glucose is negative. Urine osmolality rises to 560 mOsm/kg after desmopressin.
oneliner: 12M + new enuresis + 10-15 voids/day + 7.6 L/day + urine osm 230 + serum osm 302 + responds to desmopressin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: serum osmolality would be **low**; his is high
whyNot.C: urine **would not concentrate** after desmopressin
whyNot.D: **urine glucose is negative**
whyNot.E: would give **concentrated urine and low serum osmolality**

why: **Polyuria of 7.6 L/day** with **dilute urine despite high serum osmolality** that corrects with desmopressin = hypothalamic ADH deficiency.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has polydipsia and polyuria. After 8 hours of water deprivation her urine osmolality stays at 100 mOsm/kg, but it rises to 450 after desmopressin.
oneliner: 30F + polydipsia + polyuria + urine osm stuck at 100 after water deprivation → 450 after desmopressin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: urine would **concentrate with water deprivation alone**
whyNot.B: urine would **stay dilute even after desmopressin**
whyNot.C: would show **glycosuria and concentrated urine**
whyNot.D: urine would already be **concentrated**, with hyponatremia

why: Urine that **fails to concentrate with deprivation** but **concentrates with desmopressin** separates central from nephrogenic DI.

stem: A 25-year-old man has thirst, blurred vision and passes urine many times at night. He is normotensive, has no edema, and his creatinine and glucose are normal. Serum sodium is 160 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 165 mOsm/kg.
oneliner: 25M + thirst + nocturia + blurred vision + Na 160 + urine osm 165 + normal creatinine and glucose → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: gives **hyponatremia** with concentrated urine
whyNot.B: would cause **hypertension and hypokalemia**; he is normotensive and the polyuria is dilute
whyNot.D: **creatinine is normal** and urine output is high, not low
whyNot.E: would show **edema and dilutional hyponatremia**

why: **Hypernatremia with polyuria and inappropriately dilute urine** (osmolality 165) in a patient with normal glucose and creatinine = diabetes insipidus.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with bipolar disorder has had her lithium dose raised over recent months. She now has marked thirst and passes 6.5 L of urine daily. Serum sodium is 151 mEq/L, glucose is normal, and urine osmolality is 75 mOsm/kg. Urine osmolality does not change after desmopressin.
oneliner: 45F + bipolar on lithium (dose raised) + thirst + 6.5 L urine/day + Na 151 + urine osm 75 + no response to desmopressin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: urine **would concentrate** with desmopressin
whyNot.C: sodium would be **low-normal**, not 151
whyNot.D: her **glucose is normal**
whyNot.E: presents with **hematuria and flank pain**, not isolated dilute polyuria

why: **Lithium exposure** with dilute polyuria that **does not respond to desmopressin** = collecting-duct resistance to ADH.

stem: A 22-year-old man has had thirst and large-volume urination since early childhood, and a maternal uncle has the same problem. He is now dehydrated and fatigued. Serum sodium is 150 mEq/L, plasma ADH is elevated, and urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg and does not rise after desmopressin.
oneliner: 22M + lifelong polyuria + polydipsia + maternal uncle affected + dehydration + Na 150 + high ADH + urine osm 90, no response to desmopressin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: ADH would be **low**, and urine would respond to desmopressin
whyNot.B: he is **dehydrated with high sodium**, not overhydrated
whyNot.C: no hyperglycemia or **osmotic diuresis** is described; urine is very dilute
whyNot.E: would give **hyponatremia and concentrated urine**

why: **High ADH with dilute urine that does not respond to desmopressin** = kidney unresponsive to ADH (X-linked V2 receptor defect).

stem: A 62-year-old man is lethargic and mildly confused. He has no edema and normal skin turgor, and his blood pressure is normal. Laboratory results: serum sodium 125 mEq/L, serum osmolality 258 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 45 mEq/L. TSH and morning cortisol are normal.
oneliner: 62M + lethargy + euvolemic + Na 125 + serum osm 258 + urine osm 520 + urine Na 45 + normal TSH and cortisol → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **cortisol is normal**
whyNot.C: **TSH is normal**
whyNot.D: urine would be **maximally dilute**, not 520
whyNot.E: he is **euvolemic**, not volume depleted

answer: SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion)
why: **Low serum osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine** in a euvolemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function = SIADH.

stem: A thin 72-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history is confused. Sodium is 118 mEq/L, urine osmolality is 600 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium is 50 mEq/L; he has no edema and normal jugular venous pressure.
oneliner: 72M + 50 pack-years + confusion + Na 118 + urine osm 600 + urine Na 50 + euvolemic → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: urine would be **dilute**, not 600
whyNot.B: gives **hypernatremia** with dilute urine
whyNot.C: would show **low urine sodium and volume depletion**
whyNot.D: would have **edema and raised jugular venous pressure**

why: **Hyponatremia with concentrated urine and high urine sodium** in a euvolemic patient (smoker, likely lung tumor) = SIADH.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has a painless 2-cm midline neck mass just below the hyoid bone, present since infancy, that moves upward when he sticks out his tongue.
oneliner: 4M + painless midline neck mass below hyoid + since infancy + rises on tongue protrusion → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: a **lateral** neck mass along the sternocleidomastoid; this is midline
whyNot.B: usually sits at the **tongue base** (lingual thyroid), often with hypothyroidism, rather than as a mass below the hyoid
whyNot.D: does **not move with tongue protrusion**
whyNot.E: a soft **lateral or posterior** neck mass; this is midline

why: A **midline neck mass below the hyoid that rises with tongue protrusion** = remnant of the thyroglossal duct from the foramen cecum.

stem: A newborn boy has a midline mass at the base of the tongue and mild feeding difficulty. Neck ultrasound shows no thyroid tissue in its usual position in front of the trachea. The newborn screening TSH is elevated.
oneliner: newborn M + midline tongue-base mass + feeding difficulty + no thyroid in neck on ultrasound + high TSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: a **neck mass below the hyoid** with a normally placed thyroid, not a tongue-base mass
whyNot.C: a **lateral** neck swelling; this mass is at the tongue base
whyNot.D: a **translucent floor-of-mouth cyst** from the sublingual gland, with a normal thyroid
whyNot.E: a **non-thyroid** cyst; it would not explain the absent neck thyroid and high TSH

why: A **tongue-base mass** with **no thyroid in the neck** and high TSH = failed descent of the thyroid from the foramen cecum.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has fatigue, cold intolerance and weight gain. Achilles reflexes show delayed relaxation. No thyroid tissue can be felt in the neck, and her TSH is elevated. A radioiodine scan is shown.
oneliner: 34F + fatigue + cold intolerance + weight gain + slow reflex relaxation + no palpable thyroid + high TSH + [radioiodine scan] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: usually a **goiter with uptake in the neck** rather than a single focus at the tongue base
whyNot.B: a **non-functioning cyst** that does not take up iodine, with the thyroid still in the neck
whyNot.C: a **hyperthyroid** state with diffuse neck uptake; she is hypothyroid
whyNot.D: would show **no uptake anywhere**; the scan shows a focus

why: **Hypothyroid features** with **radioiodine uptake at the tongue base and none in the neck** = ectopic thyroid tissue.

image.prompt: Anterior and lateral radioiodine thyroid scan of the head and neck showing a single focus of tracer uptake at the base of the tongue and no uptake in the usual location in the anterior neck. No labels or text.

stem: A 3-week-old girl has been lethargic and feeding poorly. Her jaundice has lasted since birth. She has a hoarse cry, low muscle tone and a cool body temperature. Examination shows a large tongue and an umbilical hernia, with no other dysmorphic features.
oneliner: 3-wk F + lethargy + poor feeding + prolonged jaundice + hoarse cry + hypotonia + large tongue + umbilical hernia + no dysmorphic features → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: also gives hypotonia and umbilical hernia, but she has **no dysmorphic features** (upslanting eyes, flat face, single palmar crease)
whyNot.C: presents with **ambiguous genitalia or salt wasting**, not macroglossia and hoarse cry
whyNot.D: **hyperthyroid**: irritability, tachycardia and goiter, not lethargy and hypothermia
whyNot.E: causes **regression and a cherry-red macula** at several months, not macroglossia and prolonged jaundice

why: **Prolonged jaundice, hoarse cry, macroglossia and umbilical hernia** with lethargy and hypotonia = congenital hypothyroidism.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has taken the same levothyroxine dose every morning for 6 years, with a normal TSH. She reports no missed doses. Two months ago she started calcium carbonate for bone health, taking it with her thyroid pill. She is now tired and constipated. TSH is 14 mU/L and free T4 is low. She takes no other new medications.
oneliner: 50F + hypothyroid on stable levothyroxine x6 y + calcium carbonate added 2 mo ago + symptoms back + high TSH + low FT4 → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her laboratory changes?

options.C: Increased levothyroxine clearance by an enzyme inducer
options.D: Undertreated hypothyroidism from impaired levothyroxine absorption

whyNot.A: she reports **no missed doses**, and the change followed a new drug
whyNot.B: would drift **gradually over years**, not abruptly after starting calcium
whyNot.C: she takes **no inducer** such as rifampin or phenytoin
whyNot.E: free T4 is **low**, so this is overt

answer: Hypothyroidism from reduced levothyroxine absorption (calcium carbonate)
why: **Calcium carbonate started** while on a long-stable dose, then **high TSH with low free T4** = calcium binds levothyroxine in the gut.

stem: A 68-year-old man is brought in by his wife because he has become apathetic and slow to speak over several months. He has gained weight and is constipated. He complains that his memory is poor. His tongue looks enlarged and his voice is hoarse.
oneliner: 68M + apathy + slow speech + weight gain + constipation + memory complaints + enlarged tongue + hoarse voice → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: would not explain **constipation, weight gain, enlarged tongue or hoarseness**
whyNot.B: does not cause an **enlarged tongue or hoarse voice**
whyNot.D: would show **Argyll Robertson pupils or tabes dorsalis** features, not macroglossia
whyNot.E: needs the triad of **gait disturbance and urinary incontinence**; none described

why: **Psychomotor slowing with constipation, weight gain, hoarseness and enlarged tongue** = hypothyroidism presenting as pseudodementia.

stem: A 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease has dry skin, marked cold intolerance and constipation for several months. His heart rate is 52/min and the relaxation phase of his ankle reflexes is slow. Hemoglobin and creatinine are normal.
oneliner: 70M + diabetes + dry skin + cold intolerance + constipation + HR 52 + slow reflex relaxation + normal Hb and creatinine → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: does not cause **bradycardia, dry skin or delayed reflex relaxation**
whyNot.C: **hemoglobin is normal**
whyNot.D: **creatinine is normal**
whyNot.E: would give **orthostasis and fixed heart rate**, not dry skin, cold intolerance and slow reflexes

why: **Cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, bradycardia and delayed reflex relaxation** = hypothyroidism.

stem: A 44-year-old woman has a hoarse voice, constipation and slow relaxation of her ankle reflexes. Free T4 is 0.4 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8) and TSH is 0.4 mU/L (normal 0.5-5). After TRH injection, TSH rises briskly.
oneliner: 44F + hoarse voice + constipation + slow reflex relaxation + low FT4 + low TSH → brisk rise after TRH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: TSH would be **high** with low free T4
whyNot.C: TSH **would not rise** after TRH
whyNot.D: free T4 would be **high or normal** with normal-high TSH
whyNot.E: would give a **raised TSH**, not a low one

why: **Low free T4 with low TSH** that **responds to TRH** = pituitary intact, TRH deficiency from the hypothalamus.

stem: A 41-year-old woman has fatigue, cold intolerance and dry skin. Her thyroid is diffusely enlarged, firm and nontender. A biopsy specimen of the gland is shown.
oneliner: 41F + fatigue + cold intolerance + dry skin + firm nontender goiter + [thyroid biopsy] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: presents with **hyperthyroid features**; she is hypothyroid
whyNot.B: a **painful, tender** gland; hers is nontender
whyNot.C: presents as a **discrete nodule**, not a diffuse hypothyroid goiter
whyNot.D: a **stony-hard, fixed** gland; hers is firm but not fixed

why: **Hypothyroid features with a firm nontender goiter** and a **lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers** = Hashimoto thyroiditis.

image.prompt: H&E-stained thyroid tissue showing a dense lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate with lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, and atrophic thyroid follicles lined by large pink Hurthle cells. No labels or text.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is nervous and sweaty and cannot tolerate heat. She has a wide-eyed stare, a fine tremor, warm moist skin, a heart rate of 110/min and a diffuse nontender goiter.
oneliner: 27F + nervous + heat intolerance + stare + tremor + warm moist skin + HR 110 + diffuse goiter → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: usually **hypothyroid** with a firm goiter
whyNot.B: a **nodular** gland in older patients, not diffuse in a young woman with stare
whyNot.C: needs **fever, delirium and cardiovascular collapse**; none are described
whyNot.E: does not cause a **diffuse goiter, warm moist skin or stare**

why: **Stare, tremor and warm moist skin** with a **diffuse goiter** in a young woman = Graves disease.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with weight loss and palpitations has proptosis, a suppressed TSH and a high free T4. Radioiodine uptake is diffusely increased.
oneliner: 29F + weight loss + palpitations + proptosis + low TSH + high FT4 + diffuse high uptake → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: uptake would be **low**, with a painful gland
whyNot.B: uptake is **patchy** in several nodules, and there is no proptosis
whyNot.D: not hyperthyroid with **diffusely high uptake**
whyNot.E: uptake is **low**, and there is no proptosis

why: **Proptosis** and **diffusely increased uptake** with thyrotoxicosis = Graves disease (TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies).

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation has anxiety, palpitations, tremor and loose stools. She has gained little weight despite a good appetite. Her skin is warm and moist, her thyroid is diffusely enlarged and her heart rate is 112/min. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is high. She is normotensive.
oneliner: 30F + 20 wk pregnant + anxiety + palpitations + tremor + loose stools + poor weight gain + diffuse goiter + low TSH + high FT4 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: does not produce a **high free T4, diffuse goiter or tremor**
whyNot.C: does not cause **abnormal thyroid tests or warm moist skin**
whyNot.D: causes **paroxysmal hypertension**, and thyroid tests would be normal
whyNot.E: limited to **early pregnancy hCG peak with hyperemesis**, without a diffuse goiter at 20 weeks

why: **Suppressed TSH with high free T4**, warm moist skin and a **diffuse goiter** arising in pregnancy = Graves disease.

stem: A 39-year-old woman with hypothyroidism takes liothyronine (T3). Believing a bigger dose would help her fatigue, she doubled it 3 weeks ago. She now has palpitations, tremor and a heart rate of 112/min, with brisk reflexes. Her thyroid is not enlarged or tender. Laboratory results: TSH <0.01 mU/L, free T4 0.5 ng/dL (low-normal), total T3 elevated, thyroglobulin low. Radioiodine uptake is low.
oneliner: 39F + hypothyroid on T3 + dose doubled + palpitations + tremor + HR 112 + brisk reflexes + low TSH + low-normal FT4 + low thyroglobulin + low uptake → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: would have a **goiter and high radioiodine uptake**, with high free T4
whyNot.B: a **tender** gland with high ESR; hers is non-tender
whyNot.D: would not give **suppressed TSH or high T3**
whyNot.E: needs a **nodule with focal uptake**, and thyroglobulin would not be low

why: **Doubled T3 dose** with **suppressed TSH, low thyroglobulin and low uptake** = thyrotoxicosis from exogenous hormone.

stem: A 47-year-old woman who had a total thyroidectomy for a benign goiter takes levothyroxine and now has palpitations, insomnia and a heart rate of 108/min. Her TSH is 0.1 mU/L.
oneliner: 47F + total thyroidectomy for benign goiter + on levothyroxine + palpitations + insomnia + HR 108 + TSH 0.1 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: does not explain the **suppressed TSH**
whyNot.C: she has **no thyroid tissue** left to be stimulated
whyNot.D: would not suppress TSH, and causes **paroxysmal hypertension**
whyNot.E: needs an **inflamed thyroid gland**, which she lacks

why: **Thyroid removed, on levothyroxine, with suppressed TSH and hyperthyroid symptoms** = over-replacement.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is seen 3 months after an uncomplicated delivery. She is breastfeeding and has palpitations, heat intolerance and irritability. She has a heart rate of 106/min, lid lag and a mildly enlarged, nontender thyroid, with no proptosis. Laboratory results: TSH 0.02 mU/L, free T4 3.1 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8), anti-TPO antibodies positive, TSH-receptor antibodies negative, ESR normal.
oneliner: 31F + 3 mo postpartum + palpitations + heat intolerance + nontender mild goiter + low TSH + high FT4 + anti-TPO positive + TSH-receptor Ab negative + normal ESR → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: would show **TSH-receptor antibodies and proptosis**; these are negative or absent
whyNot.B: a **painful gland with high ESR**; hers is nontender with normal ESR
whyNot.C: would feel as a **discrete nodule**, not a diffuse mild enlargement
whyNot.E: the usual picture is **hypothyroidism**, not an acute hyperthyroid phase after delivery

why: **Thyrotoxic symptoms within months of delivery** with a **painless goiter**, positive anti-TPO and normal ESR = postpartum thyroiditis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has had severe pain in the front of her neck, radiating to the jaw and ear, for 5 days. Two weeks earlier she had a sore throat and runny nose. She has palpitations and a low-grade fever. The thyroid is enlarged and very tender, without proptosis. TSH is suppressed, free T4 is high and ESR is 85 mm/h.
oneliner: 30F + URI 2 wk ago + severe neck pain to jaw + palpitations + low-grade fever + tender goiter + low TSH + ESR 85 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: a **painless** diffuse goiter with proptosis, not a tender gland with high ESR
whyNot.C: painless and **nodular**, in older patients
whyNot.D: usually **high fever, fluctuance and a normal thyroid hormone state**
whyNot.E: **painless**, with hypothyroid features

why: **Painful tender thyroid after a viral illness** with **thyrotoxicosis and high ESR** = subacute granulomatous thyroiditis.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has had a slowly enlarging neck swelling for 15 years. It is painless, and on examination the thyroid is enlarged with several palpable nodules; ultrasound confirms multiple nodules of different sizes. She has no heat intolerance, tremor or weight change. TSH and free T4 are normal.
oneliner: 58F + slowly enlarging painless neck swelling x15 y + multiple thyroid nodules + euthyroid → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: a **diffuse** goiter with hyperthyroid features and proptosis
whyNot.B: a **firm diffuse** goiter, usually hypothyroid
whyNot.C: a **single hard nodule** with lymph node spread, not many nodules over 15 years
whyNot.D: a **painful, tender** gland over days to weeks

why: **Long-standing painless enlargement with multiple nodules** and normal thyroid function = multinodular goiter.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has palpitations, weight loss and heat intolerance. A single 3-cm painless nodule is felt in the right lobe, and the rest of the gland is not enlarged. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is high. A radioiodine scan shows intense uptake in the nodule with almost no uptake in the remaining thyroid.
oneliner: 52F + palpitations + weight loss + single 3-cm nodule + low TSH + high FT4 + scan: uptake only in the nodule → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: gives **diffusely increased uptake** in a diffusely enlarged gland
whyNot.B: uptake is **patchy in several nodules**, not one
whyNot.D: usually a **cold (non-functioning) nodule**
whyNot.E: uptake is **low everywhere**, and the gland is painful

why: A **single nodule that takes up iodine while the rest of the gland is suppressed**, with hyperthyroidism = toxic adenoma.

stem: A 48-year-old man has right flank pain and passes a ureteral stone. He also has bone pain and fatigue and takes no medications. Laboratory results: calcium 12.3 mg/dL, phosphorus 2.0 mg/dL, intact PTH 140 pg/mL (normal 15-65), 24-hour urine calcium elevated. Hemoglobin and creatinine are normal.
oneliner: 48M + ureteral stone + bone pain + fatigue + Ca 12.3 + phos 2.0 + PTH 140 + high urine Ca → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: PTH would be **suppressed** (PTHrP acts instead)
whyNot.C: PTH would be **low**, with anemia and renal impairment; his Hb and creatinine are normal
whyNot.D: urine calcium would be **low**; his is high
whyNot.E: PTH would be **suppressed** and phosphorus high-normal

why: **Stones, bone pain and fatigue** with **high calcium, low phosphorus and inappropriately high PTH** = primary hyperparathyroidism.

stem: A 47-year-old woman has fatigue, loss of appetite and diffuse bone aches. Calcium is 11.8 mg/dL, PTH is 160 pg/mL and creatinine is normal. A radiograph of her hand is shown.
oneliner: 47F + fatigue + anorexia + bone aches + Ca 11.8 + PTH 160 + normal creatinine + [hand x-ray] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: calcium is **low-normal** with soft bones and looser zones
whyNot.B: **normal calcium and PTH**, with focal thickened bone
whyNot.C: needs **kidney failure**; her creatinine is normal
whyNot.E: PTH would be **suppressed** if calcium were high

why: **High calcium with high PTH** and **subperiosteal bone resorption** on the hand film = hyperparathyroid bone disease.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with calcium 11.6 mg/dL, PTH 150 pg/mL and normal creatinine undergoes neck exploration. Both superior glands and one inferior gland are normal in size at the back of the thyroid. The other inferior gland is not in its usual position and is eventually found as a 1-cm encapsulated nodule within the thymus in the upper mediastinum.
oneliner: 55F + Ca 11.6 + PTH 150 + normal creatinine + 3 normal glands + 4th gland absent from neck, 1-cm nodule found in thymus → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: all four glands would be **enlarged**; here three are normal
whyNot.C: a **large invasive, adherent mass** with severe hypercalcemia; this nodule is small and encapsulated
whyNot.D: causes **hypocalcemia from absent glands** in childhood, not hypercalcemia
whyNot.E: follows **long-standing kidney failure**; her creatinine is normal

why: **One enlarged gland, three normal ones**, with the fourth in the **thymus** = adenoma of an inferior gland (third pouch) that descended with the thymus.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has hypercalcemia on routine labs: calcium 11.4 mg/dL, phosphate 2.4 mg/dL, PTH 85 pg/mL (normal 15-65), normal vitamin D, and a high 24-hour urine calcium. She has no symptoms, takes no medications and has no family history.
oneliner: 58F + asymptomatic + Ca 11.4 + phos 2.4 + PTH 85 + high urine Ca + no drugs, no family history → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: urine calcium would be **low**, with a family history
whyNot.B: vitamin D is **normal** and PTH would be suppressed
whyNot.D: PTH would be **suppressed**
whyNot.E: she takes **no medications**, and urine calcium would be low

why: **Hypercalcemia with non-suppressed PTH and high urinary calcium** = primary hyperparathyroidism, not FHH.

stem: A 55-year-old obese man with hypertension has had progressive kidney disease for years. Laboratory results: creatinine 4.1 mg/dL, phosphorus 6.8 mg/dL (normal 2.5-4.5), calcium 8.2 mg/dL, PTH 450 pg/mL (normal 15-65), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D low.
oneliner: 55M + HTN + advanced CKD (Cr 4.1) + phos 6.8 + Ca 8.2 + PTH 450 + low 1,25-D → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: calcium would be **high** and phosphorus low
whyNot.C: needs **hypercalcemia** from autonomous glands after long-standing disease; his calcium is low
whyNot.D: creatinine would be **normal** and phosphorus low
whyNot.E: PTH would be **low**, not 450

why: **Advanced CKD with high phosphate, low calcium and low 1,25-vitamin D** drives a compensatory **high PTH**.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has tingling around the mouth and fingers and muscle cramps 2 days after a total thyroidectomy for Graves disease. Inflating a blood pressure cuff on her arm causes carpal spasm. Calcium is 6.9 mg/dL, phosphate is 5.6 mg/dL, magnesium is normal and PTH is low.
oneliner: 38F + 2 d after total thyroidectomy + perioral tingling + cramps + cuff-induced carpal spasm + Ca 6.9 + phos 5.6 + low PTH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: PTH would be **high**, with low phosphate
whyNot.B: PTH would be **high** (end-organ resistance)
whyNot.C: gives low calcium with **low phosphate** and high or normal PTH; here phosphate is high and PTH low
whyNot.E: **magnesium is normal**

why: **Neck surgery** with **low calcium, high phosphate and low PTH** = parathyroid injury or removal.

stem: A 41-year-old man has confusion, muscle aches, low mood and tingling around his mouth and fingertips. His skin and hair are dry and scaly. Tapping over the facial nerve in front of the ear makes his facial muscles twitch. Calcium is 6.8 mg/dL, phosphate is 6.1 mg/dL, and creatinine, TSH and potassium are normal.
oneliner: 41M + confusion + myalgias + low mood + perioral tingling + dry scaly skin + facial twitch on tapping + Ca 6.8 + phos 6.1 + normal creatinine and TSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **TSH is normal** and calcium would not be low
whyNot.C: calcium would be **high**
whyNot.D: would show **hyperpigmentation, hypotension and hyperkalemia**; potassium is normal
whyNot.E: would show **central obesity, striae and hypertension**, not a low calcium

why: **Chvostek sign, perioral paresthesias** and **low calcium with high phosphate** = PTH deficiency.

stem: A 29-year-old man has his first generalized seizure. Before it, he had tingling around his mouth and fingers. Examination shows flexion of the wrists and fingers and plantar flexion of the feet, with brisk reflexes. Calcium is 6.4 mg/dL, sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L and magnesium 2.0 mg/dL (normal).
oneliner: 29M + first seizure + perioral and finger tingling + wrist and foot spasm + hyperreflexia + Ca 6.4 + normal Na, K, Mg → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **magnesium is normal**
whyNot.B: **sodium is normal** at 138
whyNot.C: **potassium is normal**, and it causes weakness, not tetany
whyNot.D: would not explain **carpopedal spasm, paresthesias or a low calcium**

why: **Perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, hyperreflexia and a seizure** with **calcium 6.4** = hypocalcemia.

stem: A 9-year-old boy has had perioral tingling and a seizure. His father has had similar episodes. Laboratory results: calcium 7.0 mg/dL, phosphate 6.0 mg/dL, magnesium low-normal, PTH 8 pg/mL (low), creatinine normal. Urine calcium excretion is high for his serum calcium. He has no history of neck surgery.
oneliner: 9M + tingling + seizure + father affected + Ca 7.0 + phos 6.0 + low PTH + high urine calcium + no neck surgery → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: this is the **inactivating** counterpart, with **high** calcium and low urine calcium
whyNot.B: needs **neck surgery or autoimmunity**; he has no surgery, an **affected father**, and urine calcium high for his serum level
whyNot.D: PTH would be **high**
whyNot.E: PTH would be **high** and phosphate low

why: **Familial low calcium with low PTH and high urine calcium** = receptor set to sense high calcium.

stem: A 34-year-old woman lives in a northern city, covers her skin fully when outdoors and avoids sun. She drinks fortified milk daily and eats fish twice a week. She has diffuse bone aches. She has no diarrhea or weight loss. Calcium is low-normal, creatinine is normal, PTH is high and 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 8 ng/mL (low).
oneliner: 34F + sun avoidance + good dietary intake + bone aches + no diarrhea + low-normal Ca + high PTH + 25-OH D 8 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: calcium would be **high**, not low-normal
whyNot.B: would cause **diarrhea and weight loss**, and she has an adequate intake
whyNot.C: PTH would be **low**
whyNot.D: **creatinine is normal**; CKD lowers 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and raises phosphate

why: **Sun avoidance** with **low 25-hydroxyvitamin D**, high PTH and bone pain, despite adequate intake = deficiency from lack of skin synthesis.

stem: A 36-year-old woman has a round face, central obesity, wide purple striae on her abdomen and proximal muscle weakness. Her blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg.
oneliner: 36F + moon face + central obesity + wide purple abdominal striae + proximal weakness + BP 160/100 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: striae are **pale or pink** and there is no proximal weakness
whyNot.C: gives **cold intolerance and bradycardia**, not purple striae and weakness with hypertension
whyNot.D: centres on **hirsutism and irregular menses**; none described
whyNot.E: gives **weight loss and hypotension**, not obesity and hypertension

why: **Wide purple striae, moon face, central obesity and proximal weakness** with hypertension = cortisol excess.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is admitted with severe back pain after bending over; imaging shows a vertebral compression fracture. She has gained weight over the abdomen and face while her arms and legs look thin. She has wide purple striae over her abdomen. Calcium and hemoglobin are normal.
oneliner: 45F + spontaneous vertebral fracture + central weight gain with thin limbs + purple striae + normal Ca and Hb → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: would not explain **purple striae or central obesity with thin limbs**
whyNot.B: **calcium is normal**, and striae are not a feature
whyNot.D: **hemoglobin is normal**, and it does not cause striae or central obesity
whyNot.E: gives generalized fat, **not thin limbs with purple striae**

why: **Vertebral fracture with central obesity, thin limbs and purple striae** = cortisol excess (glucocorticoid-induced bone loss).

stem: A 39-year-old woman has gained 12 kg over 8 months and bruises easily. She has a round face, a fat pad on the upper back and wide purple striae on her abdomen. She takes no medications. Blood pressure is 164/98 mm Hg and fasting glucose is 130 mg/dL. Morning cortisol is 28 mcg/dL and ACTH is below 5 pg/mL (low). After 8 mg of dexamethasone at night, her morning cortisol is unchanged.
oneliner: 39F + 12 kg gain + bruising + moon face + upper back fat pad + purple striae + BP 164/98 + glucose 130 + no drugs + high cortisol + ACTH <5 + no suppression with 8 mg dex → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: ACTH would be **normal or high**, and high-dose dexamethasone would suppress cortisol
whyNot.C: ACTH would be **very high**
whyNot.D: she takes **no medications**
whyNot.E: does not give **purple striae, bruising or high cortisol**

why: **High cortisol with suppressed ACTH** that **fails to suppress** = autonomous cortisol production from the adrenal.

stem: An 11-year-old boy with asthma has taken oral prednisone daily for 14 months, with the dose increased several times. He has gained weight, has stopped growing in height and has swelling of both legs. Blood pressure is raised. Urinalysis shows no protein, and morning cortisol and ACTH are both low.
oneliner: 11M + asthma + daily oral prednisone x14 mo, dose rising + weight gain + growth failure + leg edema + HTN + no proteinuria + low cortisol and ACTH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: urinalysis shows **no protein**
whyNot.B: no **dyspnea or raised jugular venous pressure**; edema fits steroid-induced salt retention
whyNot.C: would not give **hypertension and edema with low cortisol**
whyNot.E: ACTH would be **high**; his is suppressed by the steroid

why: **Prolonged oral prednisone** with obesity, growth failure and edema, and **suppressed ACTH and cortisol** = exogenous glucocorticoid excess.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history has newly discovered small cell carcinoma of the lung. He has proximal muscle weakness and a blood pressure of 175/105 mm Hg. Potassium is 2.8 mEq/L, sodium and calcium are normal, morning cortisol is markedly elevated and ACTH is high.
oneliner: 62M + 45 pack-years + small cell lung cancer + HTN + proximal weakness + K 2.8 + normal Na and Ca + high cortisol and ACTH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: would show **hyponatremia**; his sodium is normal
whyNot.B: **calcium is normal**, and it is usually squamous cell cancer
whyNot.C: cortisol and ACTH would be **normal**, with low renin
whyNot.D: weakness **improves with repeated use** and there is no hypertension or hypokalemia

why: **Small cell lung cancer** with **hypertension, hypokalemia, weakness and high cortisol with high ACTH** = paraneoplastic ACTH production.

stem: A 67-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history has had a chronic cough and weight loss. His skin has darkened over the past few months. He has proximal muscle weakness, pitting leg edema and blood pressure of 168/100 mm Hg. Chest radiography shows a central hilar mass. Potassium is 2.8 mEq/L, glucose is 190 mg/dL, cortisol is 62 mcg/dL and ACTH is 250 pg/mL (very high). An 8-mg dexamethasone suppression test does not lower his cortisol.
oneliner: 67M + 40 pack-years + cough + weight loss + new skin darkening + weakness + edema + HTN + hilar mass + K 2.8 + high cortisol and ACTH 250 + no suppression with high-dose dex → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: cortisol usually **suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone**, and ACTH levels are lower
whyNot.B: ACTH would be **suppressed**, not 250
whyNot.C: ACTH would be **low** and there would be an adrenal mass
whyNot.E: cortisol and ACTH would both be **low**

why: **Lung mass, hyperpigmentation, hypokalemia** and **very high ACTH that is not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone** = ectopic ACTH.

stem: A 47-year-old man has had 5 months of weakness and poor appetite, with a 9-kg weight loss. His skin has darkened, most obviously in the palmar creases and old scars. Blood pressure is 74/40 mm Hg. Morning serum cortisol is 2 µg/dL, ACTH is 640 pg/mL (normal 10-60), sodium is 126 mEq/L, and potassium is 5.7 mEq/L.
oneliner: 47M + weakness, weight loss 5 mo + dark creases and scars + BP 74/40 + cortisol 2 + ACTH 640 + Na 126, K 5.7 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **ACTH is high** and skin is dark; pituitary failure gives low ACTH and pale skin
whyNot.B: **Months of symptoms**; it is acute adrenal hemorrhage with sepsis
whyNot.D: Cortisol is **low**, and BP is low, not high
whyNot.E: **Cortisol is low** and ACTH high; only aldosterone would be low here

why: **Low cortisol with high ACTH** plus **hyperpigmentation, hypotension, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia** = the adrenal cortex has failed (primary).

stem: A 45-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has had 6 months of fatigue, darkened skin, hyponatremia, and a low cortisol with a high ACTH. CT of the abdomen shows both adrenal glands to be small and atrophic, with no calcification or mass.
oneliner: 45F + hypothyroidism + fatigue 6 mo + dark skin + low cortisol, high ACTH + CT: small atrophic adrenals, no calcification → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Calcified adrenals** are expected; here there is no calcification
whyNot.C: Would enlarge the glands irregularly; **atrophic glands** do not fit
whyNot.D: **Sudden** illness with enlarged, bloody glands; here the course is 6 months and the glands are small
whyNot.E: **No mass**; both glands are small, not replaced by tumor

why: **Small symmetric adrenals** with primary failure and **another autoimmune disease** = autoimmune adrenalitis, the commonest cause in developed countries.

stem: A 54-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis took prednisone daily for 9 months. He lost his tablets and has been without them for 6 days. He now has fatigue, weakness, nausea, and aching joints. Blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg, his skin is not darker than usual, potassium is 4.2 mEq/L, and his joints are not swollen.
oneliner: 54M + prednisone 9 mo, stopped abruptly + fatigue, nausea, aches + BP 92/58 + normal K, no skin darkening → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Joints are not swollen**; low BP and nausea point elsewhere
whyNot.B: **No hyperpigmentation and normal potassium**; the adrenals themselves are intact
whyNot.C: Does not explain **low blood pressure** and nausea
whyNot.E: Does not explain the **abrupt onset after stopping steroid** and the low BP

why: **Months of prednisone then sudden stop** with low BP and normal potassium = suppressed ACTH, atrophic adrenals, no cortisol.

stem: A newborn has ambiguous genitalia: an enlarged phallus-like clitoris and fused labia, with no palpable gonads. Karyotype is 46,XX. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone is markedly elevated. Blood pressure is normal and potassium is 4.6 mEq/L.
oneliner: Newborn + ambiguous genitalia, no palpable gonads + 46,XX + high 17-OHP + normal BP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Gives **no virilization** in a 46,XX infant
whyNot.C: Occurs in **46,XY**
whyNot.D: Occurs in **46,XY** with palpable testes
whyNot.E: **Hypertension and hypokalemia** expected; BP is normal here and 17-OHP is not the main rise

why: **46,XX virilized genitalia + high 17-hydroxyprogesterone** = 21-hydroxylase block with androgen excess.

stem: A 7-day-old girl is lethargic and feeding poorly. She has an enlarged clitoris with partly fused labia, and her skin is dry with poor turgor. Sodium is 122 mEq/L and potassium is 6.8 mEq/L. A pelvic ultrasound shows a uterus and ovaries.
oneliner: 7d girl + enlarged clitoris + dehydration + Na 122, K 6.8 + uterus and ovaries on US → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Would **not virilize** the genitalia
whyNot.B: Very unlikely at 7 days, and does not cause **salt wasting**
whyNot.C: Gives **hypertension and low potassium**, not hyperkalemia
whyNot.E: Genitalia are **not virilized** (female appearance in both sexes)

why: **Virilized female infant + hyponatremia and hyperkalemia** = androgen excess with cortisol and aldosterone loss.

stem: A 10-day-old boy has vomiting, poor feeding, and dehydration. Sodium is 123 mEq/L, potassium is 6.4 mEq/L, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone is high.
oneliner: 10d boy + vomiting + dehydration + Na 123, K 6.4 + high 17-OHP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Causes **low chloride, low potassium alkalosis**; potassium here is high
whyNot.C: Causes **hypertension, low potassium** and a female phenotype in XY infants
whyNot.D: **17-OHP would be low**
whyNot.E: Causes **hypertension and low potassium**

why: **Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and high 17-OHP** in a vomiting newborn = salt-losing 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

stem: A 15-year-old girl has hirsutism, an enlarged clitoris, and deepening voice. Blood pressure is 158/98 mm Hg and potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. Renin and aldosterone are low, and 11-deoxycorticosterone is high.
oneliner: 15F + virilization + BP 158/98 + K 3.0 + low renin, aldosterone + high 11-deoxycorticosterone → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Would give **no virilization**; sex steroids are low
whyNot.C: Gives **salt wasting and low BP**
whyNot.D: Aldosterone would be **high**, and no virilization
whyNot.E: Gives **low BP and high potassium** (salt wasting)

why: **Virilization + hypertension + hypokalemia + high 11-deoxycorticosterone** = block before cortisol with mineralocorticoid excess.

stem: A 45-year-old man has headaches and blood pressure of 168/104 mm Hg on repeat checks. He has no striae, no central obesity, and no episodic symptoms. Serum potassium is 2.6 mEq/L and bicarbonate is 33 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity is undetectable, aldosterone is elevated, and 24-hour urinary cortisol is normal.
oneliner: 45M + BP 168/104 + K 2.6 + HCO3 33 + renin undetectable, aldosterone high + normal urine cortisol → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Urinary cortisol is normal** and no cushingoid features
whyNot.C: Would give **low BP and high potassium**
whyNot.D: Renin is usually **high or normal**, not undetectable
whyNot.E: No **episodic spells**; aldosterone, not catecholamines, is raised

why: **Hypertension + low potassium + metabolic alkalosis + suppressed renin with high aldosterone** = autonomous aldosterone secretion.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has episodes of pounding headache, palpitations, and sweating that last about 20 minutes and are triggered by bending or lifting. During one episode her blood pressure was 185/115 mm Hg. Between episodes it is 118/76 mm Hg. Potassium and TSH are normal.
oneliner: 28F + episodic headache, palpitations, sweating + BP 185/115 in spells, 118/76 between + normal K, TSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **TSH is normal** and symptoms are not constant
whyNot.C: BP is **persistently raised**, not episodic
whyNot.D: Would show **persistent hypertension** with weak leg pulses
whyNot.E: Hypertension is **sustained with low potassium**

why: **Paroxysmal hypertension with headache, palpitations and sweating** and normal BP between spells = episodic catecholamine release.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has labile blood pressure with spells of palpitations and sweating, and is started on propranolol. Within days her blood pressure rises to 220/130 mm Hg with severe headache. Potassium is normal, she has no striae or central obesity, and CT shows a 2-cm right adrenal nodule.
oneliner: 38F + labile BP with sweaty, palpitating spells + crisis after propranolol + normal K + 2-cm adrenal nodule → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Sustained hypertension with low potassium**; potassium here is normal and BP is labile
whyNot.B: **Cushingoid features** such as striae and central obesity; she has none
whyNot.C: Does not explain **spells, a crisis after a beta blocker, or an adrenal nodule**
whyNot.E: Does not explain a **hypertensive crisis after a beta blocker** or an adrenal mass

why: **Labile BP with spells + adrenal nodule**, with a crisis after a beta blocker (unopposed alpha stimulation) = pheochromocytoma.

stem: A 10-year-old boy has had 3 weeks of frequent urination, constant thirst, and tiredness, with a 3-kg weight loss. His BMI is at the 14th percentile and he has no skin changes. Fasting glucose is 350 mg/dL and urine dipstick shows glucose.
oneliner: 10M + polyuria, thirst, tired 3 wk + weight loss + slim + glucose 350 + glucosuria → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: He is **thin with rapid onset and weight loss**, not obese with acanthosis
whyNot.C: Serum glucose would be **normal**
whyNot.D: Urine would be **dilute with no glucose**, and serum glucose normal
whyNot.E: Would be **mild, slowly progressive**, with a strong family history

why: **Child with polyuria, thirst, weight loss, glucose 350 and glucosuria** = insulin deficiency from autoimmune beta-cell loss.

dx: Hypoglycemia from insulin excess in type 1 diabetes
stem: A 6-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes has been waking at night restless, sweating, and confused. The episodes pass on their own after a short time. His father recently increased both of his insulin doses because daytime readings were high. A fingerstick during one episode was 38 mg/dL, and urine ketones were negative.
oneliner: 6M + T1DM, father raised both insulins + night restlessness, sweating, confusion + glucose 38 + no ketones → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Glucose is **low and ketones are negative**
whyNot.C: The child is **confused with a glucose of 38**, which a night terror would not explain
whyNot.D: Cause is clearly **excess insulin**; no hypotension or electrolyte change
whyNot.E: **Low glucose** explains the episodes; no postictal state or tonic-clonic activity

why: **Higher insulin doses + night sweating and confusion + glucose 38** = insulin-induced hypoglycemia.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has had type 1 diabetes for 15 years and takes multiple daily insulin injections. She has twice fainted with no sweating, tremor, or palpitations beforehand. Glucose at the second event was 32 mg/dL, and C-peptide was undetectable.
oneliner: 34F + T1DM 15 y on insulin + fainting twice with no warning sweats or tremor + glucose 32 + C-peptide undetectable → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Does not explain a **glucose of 32**
whyNot.C: **C-peptide would be high**; she injects insulin
whyNot.D: Glucose is **low**, not high
whyNot.E: Fainting with **low glucose** and no convulsive features

answer: Hypoglycemia unawareness (loss of adrenergic warning symptoms)
why: **Long-standing T1DM + hypoglycemic faints without warning symptoms** = blunted counterregulatory epinephrine response.

stem: A 12-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes takes evening NPH insulin. Several mornings a week his fasting glucose is 290 mg/dL. His mother checked a 3 AM reading when he was sweaty and tremulous: it was 46 mg/dL. His urine ketones are negative.
oneliner: 12M + T1DM, evening NPH + 3 AM glucose 46, shaky + fasting 290 + no ketones → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Ketones are negative** and he had overnight low glucose
whyNot.B: Overnight glucose would be **normal**, not 46
whyNot.D: Would not cause an **overnight low**
whyNot.E: Glucose needs would be **lower**, not high in the morning

answer: Somogyi effect (rebound hyperglycemia after nocturnal hypoglycemia)
why: **Night-time hypoglycemia followed by high fasting glucose** = counterregulatory glucagon and epinephrine overshoot.

stem: A 7-year-old girl has had 2 weeks of heavy thirst, bedwetting, and weight loss, and now has vomiting and deep breathing. Her breath smells fruity and her mucous membranes are dry. Glucose is 612 mg/dL, pH is 7.12, urine ketones are large, and serum osmolality is 310 mOsm/kg. She has not taken any medications.
oneliner: 7F + polyuria, weight loss 2 wk + vomiting + fruity breath + glucose 612, pH 7.12, large ketones, osm 310 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: There is **acidosis with ketones** and osmolality under 320
whyNot.B: Glucose is **very high** and ketones are present
whyNot.C: Glucose would be **normal or low**
whyNot.E: **No ingestion**, and glucose of 612 is not explained

why: **Glucose 612 + ketones + acidosis (pH 7.12) + fruity breath** = DKA.

stem: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has had vomiting and abdominal pain for a day, and is now confused with deep, rapid breathing. Labs show glucose 900 mg/dL, pH 7.14, bicarbonate 7 mEq/L, anion gap 28 mEq/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, and strongly positive serum ketones. Serum osmolality is 335 mOsm/kg.
oneliner: 24M + T1DM + vomiting, confusion, Kussmaul breathing + glucose 900, pH 7.14, HCO3 7, gap 28, ketones + → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Bicarbonate is **7 with a high gap and ketones**; HHS has little acidosis
whyNot.C: **Strongly positive ketones and glucose of 900** point to ketoacidosis
whyNot.D: Glucose is usually **low or normal**
whyNot.E: Does not explain **glucose 900 with ketones** in a known type 1 diabetic

why: **Type 1 diabetes + glucose 900, bicarbonate 7, high anion gap and ketones** = DKA.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with well-controlled type 1 diabetes has had 3 days of fever and a productive cough. She is now stuporous, with deep rapid breathing. Glucose is 540 mg/dL, pH is 7.08, and serum ketones are strongly positive. Blood pressure and lactate are normal.
oneliner: 22F + well-controlled T1DM + fever, productive cough 3 d + stupor, deep breathing + glucose 540, pH 7.08, ketones + → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: There is **marked ketoacidosis**, with pH 7.08
whyNot.C: Glucose is **540**
whyNot.D: **Blood pressure and lactate are normal**; ketones explain the acidosis
whyNot.E: Would cause **slow breathing**, not Kussmaul breathing

why: **Type 1 diabetes + infection + ketoacidosis with stupor** = infection raised insulin needs, causing DKA.

stem: A 52-year-old man with a BMI of 31 kg/m2 has no symptoms. At a screening visit his fasting glucose is 142 mg/dL, and 151 mg/dL a week later. HbA1c is 7.2%. C-peptide is high, and anti-GAD antibodies are negative. His father and a brother have the same condition.
oneliner: 52M + BMI 31 + fasting glucose 142, 151 + HbA1c 7.2% + high C-peptide + GAD negative + father, brother affected → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Glucose is **above 126** twice and HbA1c above 6.5%
whyNot.C: Onset at **52 with obesity**, not before 25
whyNot.D: Describes a cluster; this glucose already **meets diabetes criteria**
whyNot.E: **C-peptide is high and GAD is negative**; he is obese

why: **Two fasting glucoses over 126, HbA1c over 6.5%, obesity, high C-peptide** = type 2 diabetes.

stem: A 51-year-old woman has gained 9 kg over the past year. Her fasting glucose is now 148 and 156 mg/dL on two occasions, and HbA1c is 7.1% (5.7% a year ago). She has no striae, easy bruising or proximal weakness, and an overnight 1-mg dexamethasone test suppresses cortisol normally. C-peptide is high.
oneliner: 51F + 9 kg weight gain + fasting glucose 148, 156 + HbA1c 5.7 → 7.1% + no striae, normal dexamethasone suppression + high C-peptide → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **High C-peptide** means insulin is still being made
whyNot.B: **Normal dexamethasone suppression** and no striae or bruising
whyNot.D: Begins **before 25 in lean people** with a strong family history; not new diabetes after weight gain at 51
whyNot.E: **C-peptide would be low** after pancreatic damage; here it is high

why: **Weight gain + new diabetic-range glucose + high C-peptide**, with normal cortisol suppression = type 2 diabetes (insulin resistance).

stem: A 49-year-old long-distance truck driver has a BMI of 34 kg/m2. He eats mostly fast food on the road and often skips glucose checks. He takes one oral agent. HbA1c is 10.0%, urine ketones are negative, C-peptide is high, and GAD antibodies are negative.
oneliner: 49M + trucker, fast food + BMI 34 + HbA1c 10.0% on one oral agent + C-peptide high + GAD neg + no ketones → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **GAD is negative and C-peptide is high**
whyNot.B: **Obese with preserved C-peptide** and no ketones
whyNot.D: Onset in the late 40s with **obesity** is not typical
whyNot.E: No **bronze skin or iron overload**; obesity and diet explain the glucose

why: **Obesity + high C-peptide + negative GAD + poor control on diet and one drug** = type 2 diabetes.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with a BMI of 22 kg/m2 had gestational diabetes in her pregnancy last year. Her mother has had mild diabetes since age 25, and her sister also had gestational diabetes. Six months after delivery her fasting glucose is 118 to 125 mg/dL and HbA1c is 6.3%, with no symptoms or ketones. GAD antibodies are negative.
oneliner: 29F + BMI 22 + GDM last year + mother mild diabetes since 25, sister GDM + persistent mild fasting glucose 118-125 postpartum + GAD neg → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **GAD negative, no ketones**, and mild glucose elevation
whyNot.B: **Lean, young, with a multigenerational pattern**
whyNot.D: Hyperglycemia **persists after delivery**
whyNot.E: **Bronze skin, liver disease and iron overload**; none here, and the family pattern is autosomal dominant diabetes

why: **Lean young woman + mild persistent hyperglycemia + autosomal dominant family history** = MODY (glucokinase or similar).

stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 28 weeks has no symptoms. Her HbA1c at the first visit at 8 weeks was 5.2%. A 75-g oral glucose tolerance test now shows a fasting glucose of 98 mg/dL and a 2-hour glucose of 165 mg/dL. She has no ketones in her urine.
oneliner: 26F + G1 at 28 wk + HbA1c 5.2% at 8 wk + 75-g OGTT: fasting 98, 2-h 165 + no ketones → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Normal HbA1c at 8 weeks**, so not present before pregnancy
whyNot.C: **No ketones**, no symptoms, and normal early HbA1c
whyNot.D: Fasting **98 (cutoff 92)** and 2-hour **165 (cutoff 153)** exceed the pregnancy thresholds
whyNot.E: No **family history** and normal early glucose

why: **New glucose intolerance in the second half of pregnancy** with normal early HbA1c = gestational diabetes.

stem: An 18-hour-old boy weighs 4.9 kg and has a ruddy face. He is jittery and feeding poorly. Glucose is 20 mg/dL. His mother has type 1 diabetes with poor control. He has a normal tongue and no abdominal wall defect, and his liver is not enlarged.
oneliner: 18h boy + 4.9 kg + jittery, poor feeding + glucose 20 + mother T1DM poorly controlled + normal tongue, liver → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Does not explain **macrosomia with maternal diabetes**
whyNot.C: **Liver is not enlarged**
whyNot.D: **Maternal diabetes** already explains the fetal hyperinsulinism
whyNot.E: No **macroglossia or abdominal wall defect**

why: **Macrosomia + early hypoglycemia + maternal diabetes** = fetal hyperinsulinism from maternal hyperglycemia.

stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on insulin and a sulfonylurea is found sweaty, shaky, and confused at 2 AM. He improves fully within minutes after drinking juice.
oneliner: 62M + T2DM on insulin + sulfonylurea + 2 AM sweating, shaking, confusion + full recovery minutes after juice → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: He takes **insulin and a sulfonylurea**, which explains it; no tumor needed
whyNot.B: No **hypotension or hyperpigmentation**; drugs explain the low glucose
whyNot.C: Builds over **hours to days with vomiting and deep breathing**; it would not resolve with juice
whyNot.E: Spells are **not relieved by sugar**; here juice reverses the symptoms at once

why: **Insulin plus sulfonylurea + night-time sweating, shaking and confusion that resolve with sugar** = drug-induced hypoglycemia.

stem: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 20 years has had 5 months of severe constipation that has not improved with laxatives. His abdomen is distended. He also gets dizzy on standing, with a blood pressure fall from 128/78 to 98/60 mm Hg. Colonoscopy is normal and TSH is normal.
oneliner: 66M + T2DM 20 y + constipation 5 mo unresponsive to laxatives + distension + orthostatic drop + normal colonoscopy, TSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Colonoscopy is normal**
whyNot.B: **TSH is normal**
whyNot.D: Presents in **infancy** and would not follow 20 years of diabetes
whyNot.E: Does not cause **orthostatic hypotension** or severe unresponsive distension

why: **Long-standing diabetes + refractory constipation + orthostatic hypotension** with a normal colon = autonomic neuropathy.

stem: A 52-year-old man has burning epigastric pain after meals and black stools. Ulcers have kept recurring despite H2-blocker therapy. Endoscopy shows ulcers in the duodenum and also in the jejunum, and H. pylori testing is negative. CT shows a 2-cm pancreatic mass. He has no diarrhea, rash, or hypoglycemia.
oneliner: 52M + postprandial burning pain + melena + ulcers in duodenum and jejunum, H. pylori neg + pancreatic mass → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No hypoglycemia**
whyNot.B: **No watery diarrhea**
whyNot.C: **No rash** or hyperglycemia
whyNot.E: **H. pylori negative**, and ulcers extend into the jejunum

why: **Refractory ulcers extending into the jejunum + pancreatic mass** = gastrin-secreting tumor with massive acid output.

stem: A 48-year-old man has had 5 weeks of large-volume watery diarrhea that continues when he fasts. His face is flushed, he nearly fainted today, and potassium is 2.8 mEq/L. He has not traveled and no one around him is sick. Stool osmotic gap is low and CT shows a pancreatic tail mass.
oneliner: 48M + watery diarrhea 5 wk that persists with fasting + flushing + near-syncope + K 2.8 + no travel + pancreatic mass → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Recurrent peptic ulcers** with diarrhea; no ulcer disease here
whyNot.C: **No travel or sick contacts**, and a pancreatic mass is present
whyNot.D: Gives **gallstones, steatorrhea and diabetes**, not voluminous watery diarrhea with hypokalemia
whyNot.E: Usually has **wheezing and right heart valve lesions**, not a pancreatic mass

why: **Secretory diarrhea that persists with fasting + hypokalemia + flushing + pancreatic mass** = VIP-secreting tumor.

stem: A 58-year-old man has lost 7 kg and has a migrating red blistering rash on his groin and legs. Fasting glucose is 190 mg/dL, and CT shows a pancreatic tail mass.
oneliner: 58M + weight loss + migrating red blistering rash groin/legs + glucose 190 + pancreatic tail mass → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Would cause **hypoglycemia**, not high glucose
whyNot.C: Gives **gallstones and steatorrhea**, not a migrating blistering rash
whyNot.D: Gives **recurrent ulcers**, with raised gastrin
whyNot.E: Gives **watery diarrhea and low potassium**

why: **Necrolytic migratory erythema + new diabetes + weight loss + pancreatic mass** = glucagonoma.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has a thyroid mass. Biopsy shows sheets of spindle cells in amyloid, with C-cell hyperplasia nearby. Five years ago she had an adrenal tumor removed, and her father had a similar thyroid cancer. She has no mucosal neuromas and a normal body habitus.
oneliner: 34F + thyroid mass: spindle cells in amyloid, C-cell hyperplasia + prior adrenal tumor + father similar + no mucosal neuromas → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **No mucosal neuromas or marfanoid habitus**
whyNot.C: Would show **psammoma bodies and optically clear nuclei**, not amyloid
whyNot.D: Occurs in **the elderly** with rapid growth and no amyloid
whyNot.E: Involves **pituitary, parathyroid and pancreas**, not medullary thyroid cancer

why: **Medullary thyroid carcinoma (amyloid, C-cell hyperplasia) + adrenal tumor (pheochromocytoma) + affected parent, no neuromas** = MEN 2A.

dx: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
stem: A 12-year-old boy has been at the 3rd percentile for height since age 4 and is growing about 5 cm a year. He has Tanner stage 1 pubic hair and testes of 3 mL. His bone age is 10 years. His mother is tall and had late periods. He takes a low-dose inhaled steroid for mild asthma. TSH and IGF-1 are normal.
oneliner: 12M + 3rd percentile, growth 5 cm/y + Tanner 1 + bone age 10 + tall mother with late menarche + low-dose inhaled steroid + normal TSH, IGF-1 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

whyNot.B: **Bone age is delayed**; in familial short stature it matches age and puberty is on time
whyNot.C: **Normal IGF-1 and normal growth velocity**
whyNot.D: **TSH is normal**
whyNot.E: A **low inhaled dose** with normal growth velocity does not explain the delayed puberty and family pattern

answer: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
why: **Short, prepubertal, normal velocity, delayed bone age, family history of late puberty** = late bloomer who will catch up.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought by his mother, who worries that he is short. He is at the 50th percentile for height and has a normal BMI. He is at Tanner stage 4 and has no complaints. Growth velocity and examination are normal.
oneliner: 17M + mother worried he is short + height 50th percentile + normal BMI + Tanner 4 + no complaints → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

whyNot.A: Puberty is **at Tanner 4 and height is 50th percentile**; nothing is delayed
whyNot.C: Height is **average and velocity is normal**
whyNot.D: He is **not short**
whyNot.E: **Tanner 4** shows puberty is progressing normally

why: **Height at the 50th percentile with Tanner 4 and normal velocity** = no growth disorder; the worry is the mother's.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has never had a period. She is 142 cm tall and has no breast development. She has multiple nevi and short fourth metacarpals. FSH is markedly elevated and pelvic ultrasound shows a small uterus with streak ovaries.
oneliner: 16F + no periods + 142 cm + no breast development + many nevi + short 4th metacarpals + high FSH + streak ovaries → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Breasts are **normal** and FSH is normal; no uterus
whyNot.C: FSH would be **low**, and height normal
whyNot.D: Also streak gonads, high FSH and a uterus, but **normal or tall stature without short metacarpals**
whyNot.E: Would have **breast development, a blind vagina and no uterus**

why: **Short stature + primary amenorrhea + streak ovaries with high FSH + short fourth metacarpals** = Turner syndrome.

stem: A 13-year-old boy is teased about small, tender nodules under both nipples. He is at Tanner stage 3, growth is normal, and the testes are of normal size with no mass.
oneliner: 13M + small tender bilateral subareolar nodules + Tanner 3 + normal testes + normal growth → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Testes would be small and firm**
whyNot.C: **No testicular mass**
whyNot.D: Rare in boys, and these are **small, bilateral, tender nodules** at mid-puberty
whyNot.E: No **galactorrhea or visual symptoms**

why: **Bilateral small tender subareolar nodules at mid-puberty with normal testes** = physiologic pubertal gynecomastia.

stem: A 31-year-old man with hypopituitarism has been on hCG injections three times a week for 6 weeks to restore fertility. He takes no other medications. He now has bilateral breast swelling and tenderness. Testes are normal in consistency without a mass, and he has no nipple discharge or visual changes.
oneliner: 31M + hypopituitarism on hCG injections 6 wk, no other drugs + bilateral breast swelling, tender + normal testes, no discharge, no visual change → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his breast enlargement?

whyNot.B: **No galactorrhea or visual changes**
whyNot.C: Testes are **normal**, and this started after hCG
whyNot.D: **No testicular mass**
whyNot.E: He takes **no other medications**; hCG started just before

answer: Gynecomastia due to hCG (aromatization of testosterone to estradiol)
why: **Breast enlargement starting weeks after hCG injections** = drug-induced gynecomastia (hCG acts like LH, raising testosterone that is aromatized to estradiol).

stem: A 24-year-old woman has had a cycle every 45 to 90 days since menarche. She has facial hair and acne, a BMI of 33 kg/m2, and velvety dark skin in her axillae. Total testosterone is 78 ng/dL (normal 15-70) and DHEA-S is normal. TSH, prolactin, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and 24-hour urinary cortisol are normal.
oneliner: 24F + cycles every 45-90 d + hirsutism, acne + BMI 33 + acanthosis + mild high testosterone + normal DHEA-S, TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP, urine cortisol → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Urinary cortisol is normal** and no striae or bruising
whyNot.B: **TSH is normal**
whyNot.D: **17-hydroxyprogesterone is normal**
whyNot.E: Testosterone is **only mildly raised** and onset was gradual

why: **Oligomenorrhea + hirsutism + obesity + insulin resistance, with other causes excluded** = PCOS.

stem: A 44-year-old woman has a BMI of 36 kg/m2, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension. Her periods are regular, she has no hirsutism, striae or bruising, and she has no history of head injury or brain surgery. TSH and a 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test are normal.
oneliner: 44F + BMI 36 + T2DM + hypertension + regular periods, no striae + no head injury + normal TSH and dexamethasone suppression → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **TSH is normal**
whyNot.C: **Regular periods** and no hirsutism
whyNot.D: **No history of head injury, surgery or tumor**
whyNot.E: **Dexamethasone suppression is normal** and there are no striae

why: **BMI over 35 with normal TSH and cortisol suppression** = simple (primary) obesity driving diabetes and hypertension.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 14 mL/min/1.73 m2) is fatigued and pale. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL with MCV 88 fL. Ferritin and transferrin saturation are normal, and erythropoietin level is inappropriately low. The reticulocyte count is low.
oneliner: 58F + CKD eGFR 14 + fatigue, pale + Hb 8.4, MCV 88 + normal ferritin, transferrin saturation + low EPO, low retics → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Ferritin and transferrin saturation are normal** and MCV is normal
whyNot.B: **Ferritin is normal, not high**; erythropoietin is low because of the failing kidney
whyNot.C: Would affect **white cells and platelets** too
whyNot.E: MCV would be **low**

why: **Normocytic anemia + low erythropoietin + low reticulocytes in advanced CKD** = anemia of CKD.
